questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
questions.direct_answer: All four are stereotype annotations that mark a class as a Spring-managed component and trigger component-scan registration. The key difference is semantic clarity and, for @Repository specifically, automatic exception translation — Spring wraps persistence exceptions into its DataAccessException hierarchy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows these are not just aliases — @Repository has real runtime behavior and the others convey intent used by tools and AOP advisors.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying all four are 'exactly the same' and missing the @Repository exception translation and the role of @Controller in Spring MVC dispatch.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that custom stereotypes can be built by composing @Component with your own annotation, and that Spring's persistence exception translation is applied via PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor.

sections.title: Why @Repository Is the Only One With Real Runtime Behavior
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is saying all four annotations are identical. They're not — and the difference isn't just naming convention. All four are **meta-annotated with `@Component`**, which means component-scan discovers them equally. But `@Repository` and `@Controller` carry real framework behavior that `@Component` and `@Service` do not.

**`@Repository`** triggers `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor`, which wraps the bean in a proxy that catches low-level persistence exceptions — `SQLException`, Hibernate's `JDBCException` — and rethrows them as Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy. This decouples your service layer from your ORM. Without `@Repository`, a `JDBCException` leaks through your service layer and your controller has to catch Hibernate-specific types.

**`@Controller`** tells Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` to scan the class for `@RequestMapping` methods. Without it (or `@RestController`), your endpoint methods won't be registered as HTTP handlers — the most confusing silent failure in Spring MVC.

`@Service` carries no runtime behavior today. It's a **semantic marker** that communicates intent: this class contains business logic. AOP pointcuts often target `@Service` classes for transaction management or logging, and architecture tools use it for dependency diagrams.

sections.title: What Each Stereotype Actually Does Beyond Component Scanning
sections.content:
The table shows that the four annotations differ on two axes: **runtime behavior** and **semantic intent**. Only `@Repository` and `@Controller` add framework-level processing that `@Component` doesn't provide.

| Annotation | Meta-annotation | Runtime Behavior | Semantic Intent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@Component` | — (base) | Component scanning only | Generic managed bean |
| `@Service` | `@Component` | None beyond scanning | Business logic layer |
| `@Repository` | `@Component` | Exception translation (SQL → `DataAccessException`) | Data access layer |
| `@Controller` | `@Component` | MVC handler mapping (`@RequestMapping` discovery) | Web/presentation layer |
| `@RestController` | `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` | Handler mapping + automatic JSON serialization | REST API layer |

The `@RestController` row is a common follow-up. It's `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody` on every method — meaning return values are serialized to JSON/XML directly instead of being resolved as view names.

sections.title: Building Custom Stereotypes — Architecture Rules as Annotations
Why @Repository's Exception Translation Actually Matters in Production Code
sections.content:
Of the four stereotypes, only `@Repository` provides runtime behavior beyond lifecycle registration: **exception translation**. When `@Repository` is present, Spring wraps the bean in a `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` proxy. Any persistence exception thrown (JDBC `DataAccessException`, JPA `PersistenceException`, Hibernate exception) is **intercepted and translated** into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy.

This matters because persistence exceptions are vendor-specific. A Hibernate `ConstraintViolationException` is different from JDBC's `SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException` — both represent the same underlying failure but require different catch blocks if not translated. With `@Repository` translation, your service layer catches `DataIntegrityViolationException` (Spring's abstraction) regardless of whether the underlying database stack is JPA, JDBC, or MongoDB.

Without `@Repository` (or without the `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` bean), exceptions propagate as vendor-specific types — your service layer is coupled to the specific persistence technology. This violates the separation between persistence and business logic that `@Repository` is designed to enforce.

In Spring Boot applications, the `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` is auto-configured. In traditional Spring applications without autoconfiguration, you must explicitly declare this bean for `@Repository` exception translation to work. This is a common gap when migrating legacy Spring XML configurations to annotation-based configurations — the annotation is present but the exception translation doesn't happen because the post-processor wasn't declared.

The practical implication for **layered architecture**: if your JPA repository throws a `DataIntegrityViolationException` and your service layer catches `DataIntegrityViolationException`, you're depending on Spring's translated exception, not JPA's. This is the right design — your service layer stays decoupled from the ORM vendor. But if you ever remove `@Repository` from your repository class (easy to do when refactoring), exception translation stops, and callers that caught Spring's `DataAccessException` subclasses start seeing raw JPA exceptions. This silent breakage is another reason `@Repository` is not just a naming convention — it carries runtime behavior that the rest of the application may depend on.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Repository` is the only stereotype with real runtime behavior** — `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` wraps it in a proxy that translates SQL/JPA/Hibernate exceptions into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy; the others are semantic markers only.
- **`@Controller` enables MVC handler mapping** — `DispatcherServlet` scans `@RequestMapping` methods only in `@Controller`-annotated classes; a REST endpoint on a plain `@Component` is silently ignored.
- **All four are meta-annotated with `@Component`** — component scan discovers all four equally; the difference is the additional framework behavior each carries, not how they are discovered.
- **`@Service` has no runtime behavior today** — it is a semantic marker for business logic; AOP pointcuts and architecture tools use it, but Spring itself treats it identically to `@Component`.
- **Custom stereotypes can compose behavior** — annotate your own annotation with `@Service` + `@Transactional` to create a `@UseCase` that registers as a bean and gets transaction management automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All four annotations — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` — are meta-annotated with `@Component`, so component scan discovers them all equally. The difference is not how they are found, it is what each one adds on top of basic bean registration.

**`@Repository`**
- The only stereotype with real runtime behavior: a `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` proxy wraps it
- That proxy intercepts Hibernate, JPA, and JDBC exceptions and rethrows them as Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy — your service layer catches one consistent exception type regardless of the ORM vendor
- Remove `@Repository` and exceptions leak as vendor-specific types through the service layer

**`@Controller`**
- Tells Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` to scan the class for `@RequestMapping` methods
- Without it, your `@GetMapping` endpoint is silently ignored — the most confusing silent failure in Spring MVC
- `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` on every method

**`@Service` and `@Component`**
- `@Service` carries no runtime behavior — it is a semantic marker for the business logic layer
- AOP pointcuts and architecture analysis tools use it to identify the business layer

Start with `@Component` for generic beans, `@Service` for business logic, `@Repository` for data access (and get the exception translation benefit), `@Controller` for web endpoints. The naming communicates intent to every developer who reads the code.

sections.title: Why Your @Service Bean Wasn't Found — The Package Scan Boundary Problem
sections.content:
The most common Spring startup mystery is: 'I annotated my class with `@Service` but Spring says it doesn't exist.' The answer is almost always **component scanning didn't reach that package**.

`@ComponentScan` tells Spring which packages to scan for stereotype annotations — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, and anything meta-annotated with `@Component`. Without it, Spring doesn't know your beans exist. With `@SpringBootApplication`, you get `@ComponentScan` automatically — but it **only scans the package of the main class and all sub-packages**.

This means if your main class is in `com.example.app` and a service lives in `com.example.common.utils`, that service won't be discovered. Not because the annotation is wrong, but because the scanner never looked there. Understanding the scan boundary — and knowing how to extend it without creating a maintenance headache — is what this question tests.

The scanning process itself uses ASM bytecode reading — not class loading — to inspect annotations. This means Spring can evaluate thousands of classes without loading them into the JVM, which keeps startup fast even with broad scan boundaries.

One important nuance: `@ComponentScan` is inherited by `@SpringBootApplication`, but you can still use `@ComponentScan` explicitly on additional `@Configuration` classes to scan supplementary packages. When multiple `@ComponentScan` configurations exist in the same context, Spring merges them — both sets of packages are scanned. This is how multi-module projects can have each module's `@Configuration` class declare its own local scan, and the root application class compose them.

sections.title: How @SpringBootApplication Sets the Default Scan Boundary
Filters: Include, Exclude, and Why Scanning Too Broadly Causes Problems
sections.content:
`@ComponentScan` supports **include and exclude filters** that control which classes are registered even within scanned packages. This is useful for test configurations, multi-module projects, and preventing accidental bean registration.

```java
@ComponentScan(
    basePackages = "com.example",
    excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(
        type = FilterType.REGEX,
        pattern = "com\\.example\\.legacy\\..*"
    )
)
```

The filter types include `ANNOTATION` (exclude classes with a specific annotation), `ASSIGNABLE_TYPE` (exclude specific classes), `REGEX` (pattern-based), and `CUSTOM` (your own `TypeFilter` implementation). The `ANNOTATION` filter is the most common — for example, excluding `@Configuration` classes from a shared library that you want to import selectively.

A real-world pattern is **test isolation**. In integration tests, you might exclude certain beans that connect to external services and replace them with test doubles. `@SpringBootTest` combined with `@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = ...)` gives you precise control over which beans participate in the test context.

sections.title: Lazy Scanning, Index-Based Discovery, and the Performance Cost of Scanning Every Class in a Large Monolith
sections.content:
Component scanning works by loading every class on the classpath within the scanned packages, reading their annotations, and registering annotated classes as beans. In small projects with a few hundred classes, this is imperceptible. In a large monolith with thousands of classes, scanning can add seconds to startup time.

**`spring-context-indexer`** generates a compile-time index (`META-INF/spring.components`) listing all annotated components. At startup, Spring reads the index instead of scanning class files — dramatically faster for large codebases. Add the dependency as an annotation processor; no code changes required.

For **multi-module projects**, each module can define its own `@Configuration` class with a precise `@ComponentScan` restricted to that module's package. The root application class combines them with `@Import({ModuleAConfig.class, ModuleBConfig.class})` or relies on Spring Boot's `@SpringBootApplication` combined with module-specific auto-configuration.

**Excluding test infrastructure classes from production scans** is a common need. `@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(type = FilterType.ANNOTATION, classes = TestConfiguration.class))` prevents test-only beans from being registered in production contexts. This is essential when test helper beans (fake implementations, in-memory repositories) live in the `src/test` directory but are otherwise reachable from production classpath configurations in integration test setups.

The scanning order matters when multiple `@Configuration` classes with `@ComponentScan` are present. Spring processes them in declaration order within the configuration hierarchy — a source of subtle 'bean already defined' conflicts when two configurations accidentally scan overlapping packages.

**Detecting scan performance issues** is straightforward with `--debug` mode. The conditions evaluation report shows which configuration classes were processed and how many beans were registered. If startup is slow, the `ApplicationStartup` tracking API (Spring Boot 2.4+) lets you add `SpringApplication.setApplicationStartup(BufferingApplicationStartup)` and then query `/actuator/startup` to see exactly how long each scan and bean creation phase takes. Broad scans across packages with many classes are the most common startup performance culprit in large codebases.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootApplication` scans only the package of the main class and sub-packages** — a service in `com.example.common.utils` is invisible if the main class is in `com.example.app`; this is the most common root cause of bean-not-found errors.
- **Scanning uses ASM bytecode reading, not class loading** — Spring inspects annotations without loading classes into the JVM; broad scans stay fast but still add time when the scanned package tree is very large.
- **`spring-context-indexer` generates a compile-time component index** — adds `META-INF/spring.components` listing all annotated components; at startup Spring reads the index instead of scanning class files — measurable speedup in large monoliths.
- **`excludeFilters` prevents test beans from leaking into production** — `FilterType.ANNOTATION` can exclude `@TestConfiguration` classes that live on the test classpath.
- **Multiple `@ComponentScan` definitions are merged** — Spring combines all scanned packages from all `@Configuration` classes; overlapping packages cause duplicate bean definition conflicts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring can only inject beans it knows about — and it only knows about beans in packages it scanned. That single fact explains most of the I annotated my class but Spring says it does not exist debugging sessions.

**The default scan boundary**
- `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan` with no explicit `basePackages` — it scans the package of the main class and all its sub-packages
- A service in `com.example.common.utils` is invisible if the main class is in `com.example.app` — the scanner never reached that package
- Convention: put your main class in the root package of your project so all modules fall under the scan boundary

**How scanning works internally**
- Spring uses ASM bytecode reading — not class loading — to inspect annotations; this keeps startup fast even with broad boundaries
- `@ComponentScan` supports `includeFilters` and `excludeFilters` to control which classes register; `FilterType.ANNOTATION` can exclude test-only beans from production contexts

**Performance at scale**
- In large monoliths, scanning thousands of classes adds seconds to startup; add `spring-context-indexer` as an annotation processor to generate a compile-time component index that Spring reads instead of scanning at runtime

When something is not found, check the scan boundary first. When startup is slow, check how wide the scanned package tree is. Those two rules solve most component scan problems.
